title: Husband and Wife
attribution_note: St Theophan the Recluse (1815–1894). On the duties of husbands and wives, from Nachertanie khristianskogo nravoucheniia. Translated here fresh from the Russian for this edition. Source: https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Feofan_Zatvornik/nachertanie-hristianskogo-nravouchenija/5

pairs.en: From marriage comes temporary happiness and even eternal salvation. So one must approach it not lightly, but with fear and care. God blesses a good marriage. So be pious, devoted to God; hope in Him, pray that He Himself send you the other half, pleasing to Him and saving for you. Seeking the bond of marriage, do not have bad aims — not passionate bliss, or greed, or vanity; but that one aim which God appointed: mutual help in temporal life for the sake of eternal life, to the glory of God and the good of others. When you have found her, accept her as God's gift, with thankfulness to God, with as much love as respect for this gift.

When the choice is made, the joining must take place — a mystical fusion of spirit and body from God. A natural union, on the basis of passion, is a wild, dark union. Here it is purified, sanctified, sobered by the prayer of the Church with divine grace. It is hard to stand alone in a union that is strong and saving. The threads of nature snap. Grace is irresistible. Self-confidence is dangerous everywhere, and all the more here... So approach the sacrament humbly, with fasting and prayer.

The joined have become one flesh — and all the more, one soul. On this idea their common duties are based, namely: a strong love, not passionate but pure and sober, witnessed inwardly by mutual attachment and lively interest, as well as quick and ready sympathy, and outwardly by mutual help, so that the eye and hand of one are where the other's are. From this flow unbroken peace and unshakable harmony, preventing disagreements and quickly putting right those that happen by surprise; trust, by which each can confidently rely on the other in everything, be at ease about him in everything — whether it concerns secrets or tasks. And the crown of all is marital fidelity, that is, keeping the first condition of the union — to belong to each other alone, in soul and body. The husband is not his own, but his wife's; and the wife is not her own, but her husband's. Fidelity strengthens trust; infidelity, even only suspected, breeds jealous suspicion, which drives away peace and harmony and destroys family happiness. Not to be jealous is a sacred duty, but at the same time a feat of struggle — the art of marital wisdom and love. For here selfishness always interferes, which both demands exclusivity and fears for it. It is very laughable here and arms itself against itself.

As for the particular duties of each married person, they flow from the idea of what each of them means. The husband is head of the wife. So the husband must have and show his authority over his wife, not demean himself, not sell his headship out of cowardice or passion — for that is a disgrace to men. Only this authority must not be despotic, but loving. Have your wife as a companion, and by strong love make her obedient to you. In all matters you must count her your first, most faithful, and most sincere adviser, the first confidante of secrets. You must watch over her, care for her mental and moral perfection, gently and patiently weeding out what is bad and planting what is good, and bearing with good will and piety what is incurable in body or character. But in no way allow yourself to corrupt her by your neglect and permissiveness. A husband is a murderer if his humble, gentle, and pious wife becomes scattered, self-willed, and God-fearing no more... However, guarding her morality does not prevent satisfying her wish to carry herself decently and have dealings with outsiders — though not without his consent.

The wife, for her part, must in everything listen to her husband, incline her character to his in every way, and be wholly devoted to him, so that neither in deed nor even in thought would she venture anything without his will. So faithfully carry out all his directions, advice, and commands, not even letting the thought in that she might ever have her own way, and in nothing at all desiring or showing headship. In case of disagreement, be yielding and patiently bear everything that seems disagreeable; otherwise you will not preserve the precious peace. However, this does not take away her duty to care for her husband's good morals. By her wisdom and influence she can change his character if it is flawed; at the very least, she must not leave him in neglect, but with all the mind and strength she has, act on him and snatch him as from fire. For this, adorn herself above all with virtues, and treat other adornments as something secondary, a means, which it is easy to give up — especially when the need arises to put affairs in order. Finally, remember that her lot is the keeping of household affairs, even if only in carrying them out... Her duty is to do what is set; seeing some disorder, to speak up and put it right, or make it up.
